```{r}
# Load the coffee ratings data
coffee_ratings <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2020/2020-07-07/coffee_ratings.csv')

# Preview the data
head(coffee_ratings)

# Load package
library(tidyverse)
```

How does altitude (meters above sea level) relate to total cup points (quality score)?
Which countries produce the highest-rated coffees?
Are there any outliers or missing values to address?
What patterns emerge across different processing methods or coffee varieties?

## Looking at Total Cup Points
```{r} 
# How does altitude (meters above sea level) relate to total cup points (quality score)?
# The variable "total_cup_points" has 0 missing values, as seen in the data table
summary(coffee_ratings$total_cup_points, na.rm = TRUE)

# The mean (82.09) and median (82.50) total cup points are close to one another, suggesting a symmetric distribution. The range is from 0-90.58 points, suggesting there is a 0 point value in the data. This is strange because the 1st quartile is 81.08, super far from 0. Could this be a non-value? Will look at a boxplot and then remove the 0 value(s) to see if the distribution changes significantly.

ggplot(coffee_ratings, aes(y = coffee_ratings$total_cup_points)) + geom_boxplot() 
# This quick boxplot shows that all data points except for one are at least above 50 cup points, while one sits at 0. Judgment call would be to remove this observation from the data while analyzing total cup points.
summary(coffee_ratings$total_cup_points[coffee_ratings$total_cup_points > 0])
# Here I made a summary of total cup points without the zero value. It changes the mean and 1st quartile very slightly but not by what I think is a significant amount. Though the zero value isn't affecting the data much, I will still remove it during cleaning because it skews plots extremely far and I believe it is not an actual intended value.
```

## Looking at Altitude Variables
```{r}
# There are 4 altitude variables: "altitude", "altitude_low_meters", "altitude_high_meters", and "altitude_mean_meters". The first has 226 missing values, while the latter three have 230 missing values. 
summary(coffee_ratings$altitude) # Getting a summary of this variable brings weird results because the variable is a string, values don't have standard units. In my analysis, will use "altitude_mean_meters" because it gives the average altitude for each coffee and is in standard units of meters already. This is in meters above sea level.
summary(coffee_ratings$altitude_mean_meters, na.rm = TRUE)
# Mean (1775m) and median (1311m) are quite different, suggesting outliers skewing the mean higher. The maximum value is 190164m, which is not a possible altitude. Glancing at the column for this variable, I see there are a few observations that show values greater than the highest possible altitude on the planet (about 9000m). Because I do not know if these are typos or a wrong value, I am going to remove them from this dataset for anaylsis. Will confirm judgment through a boxplot of mean altitude.

ggplot(coffee_ratings, aes(y = coffee_ratings$altitude_mean_meters)) + geom_boxplot()

#Question: What happens to the distribution/visualization when I remove the extreme values/potential typos?

cleaned_altitude <- coffee_ratings[!is.na(coffee_ratings$altitude_mean_meters) &coffee_ratings$altitude_mean_meters < 9000,]
ggplot(cleaned_altitude, aes(y = altitude_mean_meters)) + geom_boxplot()

#This cleaned boxplot makes it a lot easier to visualize almost all of the data, as opposed to the previous boxplot, where it was impossible to see any values except for the outliers. For me, this justifies cutting those outliers from the analysis.

summary(cleaned_altitude$altitude_mean_meters)
# Now we see that the mean (1328m) and median (1311m) are much closer, suggesting the outliers were skewing the mean heavily. 
```

## Final Cleaning of Quality Score and Altitude Data
```{r}
# edit cleaned_altitude to remove the 0 value from the quality score variable, so that data is ready to analyze!
altitude_score_data <- coffee_ratings %>%
    filter(total_cup_points > 0, altitude_mean_meters < 9000) %>%
    select(total_cup_points, altitude_mean_meters)

# This data which I will now use to explore altitude and quality score, is 2 column and 1104 rows. This has excluded data with missing values, a zero value in quality score, and potential mis-entered values in altitude. 
```

## How is altitude related to cup points? 
```{r}
# First let's look at a box plot to see if the general spread, then we can split the data
ggplot(altitude_score_data, aes(x = altitude_mean_meters, y = total_cup_points)) +
    geom_point()
cor(altitude_score_data$altitude_mean_meters, altitude_score_data$total_cup_points)
# Boxplot doesn't seem to show any specific pattern, and calculating correlation seems to be pretty low (~0.15). Will randomly split the data to see if this holds up.

set.seed(67)
altitude_score_data$half <- sample(rep(c("explore", "hold out"), length.out = nrow(altitude_score_data)))
table(altitude_score_data$half)

# Let's make a scatterplot for the "explore" half
ggplot(filter(altitude_score_data, half == "explore"), aes(x = altitude_mean_meters, y = total_cup_points)) + geom_point() #has similar spread to the unsplit scatterplot

ggplot(filter(altitude_score_data, half == "hold out"), aes(x = altitude_mean_meters, y = total_cup_points)) + geom_point()
#I would judge that the scatterplots have generally the same shape and spread, so results can be predictable throughout the data and I will analyze the data as a whole set for this specific question.

# From the scatterplots, there doesn't appear to be a relatonship between altitude and quality score. What about if we convert altitude to a categorical variable with levels, what will we see?

#making cuts to turn altitude from number to category
altitude.cuts <- quantile(altitude_score_data$altitude_mean_meters, c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1), na.rm = TRUE)
altitude.cuts
altitude_score_data$mean_altitudes <- cut(altitude_score_data$altitude_mean_meters, breaks = altitude.cuts, labels = c("Low Elevation", "Middle Elevation", "High Elevation"), include.lowest = TRUE, ordered_result = TRUE)

# Will have to also make quality score a categorical variable to make a frequency table and do a chi-square test to see if altitude and score are independent.

score.cuts <- quantile(altitude_score_data$total_cup_points, c(0, 1/3, 2/3, 1), na.rm = TRUE)
score.cuts
altitude_score_data$qualitylevels <- cut(altitude_score_data$total_cup_points, breaks = score.cuts, labels = c("Lower Third Scores", "Middle Third Scores", "Higher Third Scores"), include.lowest = TRUE, ordered_result = TRUE)

altitude.vs.score <- table(altitude_score_data$mean_altitudes, altitude_score_data$qualitylevels, dnn = c("Mean Altitude (m)", "Quality Score Level"))
altitude.vs.score

# While the Lower and Middle Third Score groups do not seem to have too much variation in their distribution of elevation, I see that the Higher Third Scores group has a lot more observations in High Elevation. This makes me wonder whether altitude and score are independent, so I will perform a Chi-square test. Expected counts are all above 5, so test will be valid. 

chisquaretest1 <- chisq.test(altitude.vs.score)
round(chisquaretest1$expected, 1)
round(chisquaretest1$residuals, 1)

# Unlike the scatterplot and correlation coefficient, the chi-square test is suggesting the alternative hypothesis, which is that Mean Altitude may not be independent of Quality Score. One observation that could hint at this test result is the larger variation of score points in the Middle Elevation category. This is shown in the scatterplot. Conversely, the data points that fall in the High Elevation category do not exhibit as much variation; the points are generally at a higher score. The results of the EDA could suggest that while there is not a linear relationship between altitude and quality score, coffee grown at middle elevation may be correlated with a lot of variation in total cup points.

```

## Which Countries Produce the Highest Rated Coffees?
```{r}
# First I want to see how many countries are included in this data, to see if it would be helpful to exclude some for easier visualization.
unique(coffee_ratings$country_of_origin) #37 unique values, which includes 1 NA. 2 values are United States (Hawaii) and United States (Puerto Rico). I will keep these two as their own separate values because their climates and landscapes are different from the rest of the contiguous U.S. 

# Will make a quick bar chart to see if any of the countries stand out.
ggplot(coffee_ratings, aes(x = country_of_origin, y = total_cup_points)) + geom_col()
# This bar chart isn't really helpful since it aggregates the total cup points a country might have.
# Next idea would be to make a subset of the data that includes the top 10% of coffee scores, and then seeing where these coffees are from and visually representing that. 

toptenthreshold <- quantile(coffee_ratings$total_cup_points, probs = 0.90, na.rm = TRUE)
top_ten_scores <- coffee_ratings[coffee_ratings$total_cup_points > toptenthreshold, ]
summary(top_ten_scores$total_cup_points)
# This subsets the observations that are above the score of the 90th percentile. The lowest score above the 90th percentile is 84.75, and the highest is 90.58. 

#Which countries have coffee in the top 10%, and how many coffees in this data belong to each country listed?
top.countries <- top_ten_scores %>%
    count(country_of_origin, sort = TRUE) %>%
    slice_head(n = 5)
top.countries
# This shows there are 21 countries that have coffee in the top 10% of quality scores. That is over half of the total number of countries and still a lot to work with, so I am going to do the top 5 countries, i.e., the countries with the 5 highest count of coffee ratings in the top 10% of scores. 

top.country.ratings <- top_ten_scores %>%
  filter(country_of_origin %in% top.countries$country_of_origin) %>%
  select(country_of_origin, total_cup_points)
top.country.ratings

# The countries with the most coffees in the top 10% of quality scores are Ethiopia, United States (Hawaii), Brazil, Colombia, and Kenya.

ggplot(top.country.ratings, aes(x = country_of_origin, y = total_cup_points)) + geom_boxplot()
# Here we can see the distribution of those ratings that are from the 5 countries with the most coffees in the top 10% of scores. Ethiopia has the coffee with the highest quality score, but also the most variation in the coffees presented. Brazil also has a high median score, while Colombia seems to have the lowest of this group.
```

# Which Countries Have the Top Ten Individual Coffee Ratings
```{r}
# We saw which countries had the highest amount of coffee ratings in the top 10% of the data, but we can take a closer look to see what the top 10 actual scores are and which countries 

coffee_ratings %>%
    slice_max(order_by = total_cup_points, n = 10) %>%
    select(country_of_origin, total_cup_points)
# This code lists the top 10 coffee ratings and their country of origin. Ethiopia has 7 of the 10 top coffees in this dataset. Guatemala has the 3rd, Brazil has the 6th, and Peru has the 7th. What is interesting is that Guatemala and Peru are not in the list of 5 countries with the most coffees in the top 10% of scores, yet they have one of the highest rated coffees. Is this just a one-off good coffee from these countries, or do they have some other high rated coffees? Or generally high rated coffee overall in their country?

```

# Coffee Rating Summaries for Ethiopia, Guatemala, Brazil, and Peru
```{r}
# These are the countries that have the top 10 coffee ratings. I want to see how their mean and median coffee ratings compare to each country's top coffee. 

# summary for Ethiopia
coffee_ratings %>%
    filter(coffee_ratings$country_of_origin == "Ethiopia") %>%
    select(total_cup_points) %>%
    summary() 
# Range (80-90.58), mean (85.48), median (85.20)
# Mean and median fall within the Higher Scores category from previous section.

```

```{r}
# summary for Guatemala
coffee_ratings %>%
    filter(coffee_ratings$country_of_origin == "Guatemala") %>%
    select(total_cup_points) %>%
    summary() 
# Range (59.83-89.75), mean (81.85), median (82.50)
# Guatemala has the lowest individual coffee rating of the entire dataset. Mean and median in the Middle Score category. Seems to have a lot of variation. 
```


```{r}
# summary for Brazil
coffee_ratings %>%
    filter(coffee_ratings$country_of_origin == "Brazil") %>%
    select(total_cup_points) %>%
    summary()
# Range (70.67-88.83), mean (82.41), median (82.42). Mean and median in the Middle Score Category. Some variation as well.
```


```{r}
# summary for Peru
coffee_ratings %>%
    filter(coffee_ratings$country_of_origin == "Peru") %>%
    select(total_cup_points) %>%
    summary()
# Range (77-88.75), mean (82.53), median (82.80). Mean and median in Middle Score Category. Not as much variation as Brazil and Guatemala.
```

Overall conclusions about the countries that have the top 10 coffees is that Ethiopia seems to have, on average, the highest average coffee ratings, as well as the #1 coffee ratings. The other countries in the top 10 have more variation, with a good share of lower rated coffees as well. Some of the countries in the top 10 don't have a lot of other coffees that are in the top 10% of coffee ratings data. 


## Examining Patterns Across Varieties and Processing Methods

```{r}
#First want to look at the variables, and the levels/types of each variable
# coffee varieties
unique(coffee_ratings$variety) #29 unique values, 1 is NA. There are 226 missing values

#make a set of boxplots for the varieties, filtering out the 0 value for total cup points and removing missing values/NAs from both variables
coffee_ratings %>%
    filter(!is.na(coffee_ratings$variety), !is.na(coffee_ratings$total_cup_points), total_cup_points > 0) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = total_cup_points, y = variety)) + geom_boxplot()

# This plot doesn't tell us much about if some varieties have higher ratings, but can tell us a few things. Some of the varieties have a lot of lower rated outliers. The Catuai variety has the lowest rated coffee, while the two highest rated that are displayed are labeled Bourbon and Other. 
```
